newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EU urges Japan set single tariff on spirits.
newsitem.headline: EU urges Japan set single tariff on spirits.

text.p: The European Union said on Wednesday that Japan should set a single taxation system for domestic and imported spirits to bring its legislation in line with the rules of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

The call came in discussion in the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) on how Tokyo would implement a dispute panel report which found the present Japanese liquor tax system ran against open trade rules by favouring the national drink shochu.

Japan's trade ambassador Nobutoshi Akao told the DSB his country would make its laws conform to the finding, confirmed by an appeals panel, but said it would need time to shape the necessary measures.

Akao said he would be consulting with the EU, the United States and Canada -- who had all brought complaints to the WTO against the current tax laws -- on how long the "reasonable period" allowed under WTO rules could be.
Japan is currently preparing its budget for the 1997 fiscal year, and liquor taxes provide a significant portion of government income, Japanese officials say.

Trade sources said EU envoy Ian Wilkinson told the DSB, on which all 125 members of the WTO can sit, that Brussels wanted to see quick implementation in a case that European spirits producers argue has cost them millions of dollars in lost revenue.
Whisky producers in Scotland, who say they could have sold much more to Japan over the past few years if they had been treated equally, have warmly welcomed the panel decision.

Canada's representative Elaine Feldman said Ottawa also wanted an early move by Japan, saying too much commercial damage had been suffered by Canadian liquor exporters over the many years the current Japanese laws had been in effect.
The EU's Wilkinson said the only way for Japan to implement the panel finding was to establish a single liquor tax rate according to the degree of alcohol in a beverage, wherever it was produced.
Under the WTO's predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), Japan's liquor tax system was twice found to be in violation of open trade rules, in 1989 and 1994.

Although Tokyo altered its system both times, the three big liquor exporting powers brought a fresh case under the tighter WTO dispute procedure last year, arguing their products still faced discrimination in Japan.

Japanese officials defended the tax system, which set the rates for imported whisky as some six times the rate for shochu, by arguing the domestic beverage was largely a working class drink whose price could not be raised.
